claims.text: The initial NiFeCoCr-based alloy has a stable FCC matrix.
The initial alloy lacks metastable precipitates.
Ti or V can act as a transformation-inducing minor dopant in a NiFeCoCr-based alloy.
Adding the dopant and applying a tailored heat treatment creates a uniform dispersion of nanoscale metastable precipitates.
The nanoscale metastable precipitates occur both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The metastable precipitates undergo a stress-induced martensitic transformation during mechanical loading.
The martensitic transformation absorbs fracture energy.
The transforming precipitates cause crack deflection.
The transforming precipitates cause crack bridging.
Transformation-induced energy absorption retains or enhances toughness relative to an undoped alloy.
The doped alloy will have higher fracture toughness than the identically processed undoped baseline.
Transformation products or phase changes will be localized near crack tips in the doped alloy.
The undoped, identically processed baseline will have a homogeneous microstructure without metastable precipitates.
The proposed behavior is limited to temperatures at which the precipitates remain metastable but can undergo stress-induced transformation.
The proposed behavior is limited to dopant levels low enough to avoid significant changes to the matrix phase.
Moderately elevated temperatures can fall within the regime where the proposed transformation kinetics are active.

contradictions.description: The conditions require maintenance of a single-phase FCC structure while the intervention is explicitly designed to form metastable precipitates. If those precipitates constitute a distinct phase, the resulting material is not single-phase FCC.
